intro.html: Good sense comes in flavors. Some people are wise in the deep, slow way of long experience; some are quick and sharp; some are careful planners. And some, alas, are easy to fool or slow to catch on. This topic gives you a word for each.

Deep wisdom: sagacious, sage (a wise person). Sharp and practical: astute, shrewd, canny. Careful and sensible: judicious, prudent. Foolish: gullible (easily tricked), fatuous (smugly silly), obtuse (slow to understand).
Shrewd and canny can carry a hint of cleverness for one’s own benefit; judicious and prudent never do. They simply mean using good judgment.

words.def: wise, with sound judgment drawn from experience
words.ex: The {sagacious} old captain could read the coming weather in the clouds.
words.ctx: Faced with a hard choice, the young queen turned to her most {sagacious} adviser, who had guided the kingdom wisely through forty years of trouble.
words.etym: From Latin sagax, “keen, quick to notice,” first said of dogs with a sharp sense of smell.

mn.cue: SAGGY ears that know the way
mn.text: In the dry season, the old elephant with saggy, wrinkled ears leads the herd straight to the hidden water hole: she is {sagacious}.

scene.alt: A wise old elephant leads two young ones across the desert to a water hole.

words.def: quick to see what matters and to use it well
words.ex: An {astute} reader will notice the clue hidden in the first chapter.
words.ctx: The {astute} shopkeeper noticed that umbrellas sold out on rainy mornings, so she began setting them by the door whenever rain was forecast.
words.etym: From Latin astutus, “clever, crafty,” from astus (skill, cunning).

mn.cue: a STUDENT who spots it: a-STUTE
mn.text: The teacher’s riddle hides a trick, and Lila spots it in a second: “It’s a trick question!” She is {astute}.

scene.alt: A girl raises her hand, spotting the trick in the teacher’s riddle, while a classmate scratches his head.

words.def: sharp and clever in practical matters
words.ex: Grandma is a {shrewd} bargainer who never pays full price at the flea market.
words.ctx: Selling lemonade at the top of the steep hill instead of at the bottom was a {shrewd} move: the tired hikers there would gladly pay for a cold drink.
words.etym: From Middle English shrewe, “a nasty person,” the same word as the small animal; over time the meaning turned from nasty to sharp and clever.

mn.text: The little shrew sets up his lemonade stand at the top of the hill, right where the hikers are thirstiest: he is {shrewd}.

scene.alt: A clever little shrew sells cold drinks at the top of a hill to a hot, tired hiker.

words.def: careful and shrewd, especially with money or business
words.ex: The {canny} farmer sold her peaches in the city, where they fetched twice the price.
words.ctx: A {canny} saver, Lou kept her money in three different places, so that no single mishap could ever wipe out everything she had.
words.etym: From Scots, from can in its old sense of “to know how.”

mn.cue: she CAN’T lose it all: CAN-ny
mn.text: Nana Lou keeps her savings in three different piggy banks, so if one breaks, the rest are safe: she is {canny} with money.

scene.alt: A grandmother drops coins into three separate piggy banks.

words.ex: A {judicious} pinch of salt turned the bland soup into a delicious one.
words.ctx: The coach made {judicious} changes at halftime, resting her tired players and moving her fastest runner to defense, and the team held on to win.
words.etym: From French judicieux, from Latin judicium (judgment).
words.note: Judicious means wise in judgment, not quick to judge others.

mn.cue: JUDGE-icious: weigh it like a JUDGE
mn.text: Zoe weighs her choices like a fair judge before spending her birthday money, and picks the book she will read a hundred times: she is {judicious}.

scene.alt: A girl thinks carefully, weighing a book against a lollipop on a scale.

words.def: careful and sensible, especially about the future
words.ex: It is {prudent} to pack a flashlight before a camping trip.
words.ctx: Rather than spend his whole paycheck, Jamal thought it {prudent} to save some for the winter, when work at the farm always slowed down.
words.etym: From Latin prudens, a shortened form of providens, “seeing ahead.”

mn.cue: PRU-DENT: Pru’s car has no DENT
mn.text: Pru checks her mirrors, keeps her distance and slows down in the rain, so her old car has never had a single dent: she is {prudent}.

scene.alt: A careful driver named Pru stands proudly beside her shiny, dent-free old car.

words.def: a very wise person, respected for good judgment
words.ex: The village {sage} could settle any argument with a few calm words.
words.ctx: Young players often sought out the old coach, a {sage} whose quiet advice had helped three generations of athletes.
words.etym: From Old French sage, “wise,” from Latin sapere (to be wise).
words.note: As an adjective, sage means wise: sage advice. The herb sage has a different origin.

mn.cue: the SAGE at the top: wise old head
mn.text: The children climb all the way up the hill to ask old Edwin their hardest question, because his answers are always wise: he is a {sage}.

scene.alt: A wise old man in a toga sits on a rock giving advice to two young listeners.

words.ex: The {gullible} tourist paid twenty dollars for a “solid gold” ring made of brass.
words.ctx: Pip was so {gullible} that when his cousin told him the school had canceled Mondays, he stayed home and waited for Tuesday.
words.etym: From gull, an old word meaning to trick, or a person who is easily tricked.

mn.text: Rex sells Pip a cone of “invisible ice cream” for two dollars, and Pip happily pays: he is {gullible}.

scene.alt: A sneaky man sells a boy an empty cone of “invisible ice cream,” and the boy happily pays.

words.def: silly and pointless, in a smug way
words.ex: The host kept making {fatuous} jokes about the weather that no one laughed at.
words.ctx: Instead of answering the hard question, the speaker gave a {fatuous} reply about how everything would surely work out, smiling as though he had said something wise.

mn.cue: a smug grin and a silly idea
mn.text: Admiring himself in the mirror, Victor announces, “I am far too clever to need books!” His remark is {fatuous}: silly, and very pleased with itself.

scene.alt: A man in a top hat admires himself in a mirror and says something smug and silly.

words.def: slow to understand or to notice
words.ex: Sven was being {obtuse}; everyone else had guessed the surprise.
words.ctx: Lila hinted a dozen times that she wanted to be left alone, but her brother was {obtuse} and kept asking her to play, never noticing her sighs.
words.etym: From Latin obtusus, “blunt, dull,” from obtundere (to beat against, to blunt).
words.note: In math, an obtuse angle is wider than a right angle: more than 90 degrees. Think blunt, not sharp.

mn.cue: an OBTUSE angle: blunt, not SHARP
mn.text: Everyone shouts “Surprise!” under a giant banner with Sven’s name on it, and he still asks whose birthday it is: he is being {obtuse}.

scene.alt: Under a birthday banner with his own name, a big man scratches his head and asks whose party it is.

after.html: judicious means showing good judgment. It does not mean judging other people, and a judicious person is usually slow to criticize. obtuse also names an angle wider than 90 degrees: blunt, not sharp, which is a handy picture for a mind that is slow to catch on.

after.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: It would be {prudent} to bring a jacket; the mountains get cold after dark.

after.cap: Careful planning for what might happen is prudent.

choices: With a judicious choice of words, she calmed the angry customer.
He was so judicious that he criticized everyone he met.
The judicious puppy chewed every shoe in the house.
items.why: Judicious means showing good judgment, like choosing the right words. It does not mean quick to judge others.

items.q: Rosa believed her brother when he said that the word “gullible” is not in the dictionary. Rosa is…
items.why: She was easily fooled. (And gullible is in the dictionary.)

items.q: True or false: an obtuse person catches on very quickly.
items.why: False. Obtuse means slow to understand. Its opposite is astute or perceptive.

items.q: Which pair are closest in meaning?
items.why: Shrewd and canny both mean sharp and clever in practical matters.
